persona.name: Manoj Verma
persona.background: He spends long hours seated at a sewing machine in a warm workshop, often working late under stress to meet deadlines. He reports frequent sweating and occasional self-use of over-the-counter topical creams for skin problems.

diagnoses.name: Pityriasis versicolor (Tinea versicolor)
diagnoses.description: A relatively common persistent superficial skin condition caused by Malassezia furfur, presenting as round/oval scaly macules on the upper trunk that are usually hypopigmented on dark skin; more frequent in warm, humid climates and can be more severe/persistent in immunocompromised individuals.

diagnoses.name: Vitiligo (Nonsegmental vitiligo)
diagnoses.description: A common, slowly progressive acquired condition caused by focal loss of melanocytes, resulting in well-circumscribed depigmented macules/patches that may enlarge and coalesce; often symmetrical and occurs around orifices and on hands/feet; susceptible to sunburn.

diagnoses.name: Atopic dermatitis (Atopic eczema)
diagnoses.description: An endogenous eczema in atopic individuals characterized by extremely itchy erythematous scaly patches with scratching; may have xeroderma and vesicles acutely; chronic lesions show lichenification; distribution often periorbital and flexural areas.

diagnoses.name: Psoriasis vulgaris (Chronic plaque psoriasis)
diagnoses.description: A noninfectious chronic papulosquamous T-cell-mediated disorder with well-defined pink-red sharply demarcated plaques covered by silvery scales; commonly affects scalp and extensor surfaces; grattage test and Auspitz sign may be positive; may show Koebner phenomenon and nail pitting.

diagnoses.name: Seborrheic dermatitis
diagnoses.description: An erythematous scaling disorder affecting the nasolabial folds, eyebrows, eyelids, glabella and scalp (dandruff) in young adults (especially males); may also involve central chest and body folds; can be more common in HIV.

diagnoses.name: Erythema multiforme (EM)
diagnoses.description: An acute, self-limiting recurrent cutaneous/mucocutaneous eruption with target-shaped plaques, usually symmetrical and acral with centripetal distribution; often follows herpes infection and may include macules, papules, vesicles and bullae.

diagnoses.name: Lichen planus
diagnoses.description: A pruritic eruption described by the '5 P’s' (pruritic, planar, purple, polygonal papules/plaques) commonly on flexor wrists, shins, flanks, medial thighs and mucosa; may show Wickham’s striae and Koebner phenomenon; can leave post-lichen hyperpigmentation.

diagnoses.name: Bullous pemphigoid
diagnoses.description: A chronic relapsing blistering disorder in the elderly, typically itchy with tense bullae and usually negative Nikolsky sign; mucosal involvement occurs in a minority.

diagnoses.name: Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS)
diagnoses.description: A rare acute life-threatening mucocutaneous disease that is nearly always drug-related, characterized by erythematous dusky red atypical targetoid macules that may progress to blisters and epidermal detachment (<10% BSA in SJS) with mucous membrane involvement.

diagnoses.name: DRESS (Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)
diagnoses.description: A severe drug reaction starting as a morbilliform eruption progressing to diffuse/confluent erythema; likely when >50% BSA and/or facial edema/infiltrated lesions/scaling/purpura are present, with systemic involvement and lab findings such as leukocytosis, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis and elevated liver enzymes.

initialComplaint: “For a few months I’ve noticed light-colored patches with fine scaling on my upper chest and back. They become more noticeable after I’m out in the sun.”
medicalHistory: No documented chronic illness. He reports using an over-the-counter topical steroid cream intermittently because he thought it was an allergy; he feels the patches spread after that.
symptoms:

History suggests spread with inappropriate use of topical steroids. Living/working in a warm environment with sweating is consistent with a setting where infection is more frequent.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Pityriasis versicolor** is a superficial fungal infection caused by overgrowth of **Malassezia** on the stratum corneum. It produces multiple finely scaly macules on the upper trunk that may appear hypo- or hyperpigmented and become more apparent after sun exposure due to impaired tanning of affected skin.
keySymptoms: **Hypopigmented macules on upper trunk** - Classic distribution on chest/back; lesions stand out after tanning.
**Fine branny scaling** - Subtle scale suggests superficial stratum corneum involvement typical of Malassezia.
**More noticeable after sun exposure** - Affected areas tan poorly, increasing contrast with surrounding skin.
**Round/oval coalescing patches** - Common morphology; multiple lesions may merge into larger geographic areas.
**Warm climate and sweating** - Heat/humidity promote Malassezia proliferation and recurrence on seborrheic areas.
**Worsening/spread with topical steroids** - Steroids can alter local immunity and worsen superficial fungal overgrowth.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The patient has persistent, round/oval, finely scaly macules over the upper back, shoulders, and chest—an anatomic pattern strongly associated with **pityriasis versicolor**. The lesions are predominantly hypopigmented and become more obvious after sun exposure, consistent with reduced tanning in affected areas. The warm environment with sweating is a typical predisposing factor for **Malassezia** overgrowth. Diagnostic confirmation is supported by KOH microscopy showing the **"spaghetti and meatballs"** pattern and **Wood’s lamp** yellow fluorescence, helping distinguish it from **vitiligo** (complete pigment loss without scale).

precomputedExplanations.description: **Vitiligo** is an acquired depigmenting disorder caused by loss of functional melanocytes, producing well-demarcated chalk-white macules and patches. In **nonsegmental vitiligo**, lesions are typically symmetric and may progress over time, often without surface scale.
keySymptoms: **Chalk-white depigmented macules/patches** - Complete pigment loss with sharply defined borders, often symmetric distribution.
**No surface scale** - Lesions are smooth; fine scaling suggests an alternative diagnosis like superficial fungal infection.
**Periorificial/acral involvement** - Commonly affects face, hands, and around eyes/mouth rather than only upper trunk.
**Koebner phenomenon** - New lesions may appear at sites of trauma, friction, or pressure.
**Leukotrichia** - White hair within lesions indicates melanocyte loss and supports vitiligo.
**Autoimmune association** - Increased risk with thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, and other autoimmune conditions.
